summary: Our challenge was to create an interactive game that lets players experience designing and managing a real space mission. We answered it with Beyond Earth: The Last Hope, built in Unreal Engine 5 with C++. In 2150, humanity ignored warnings about climate change and resource depletion, and Earth became uninhabitable. The player is a commander stranded on an unknown planet. To survive, they must find local resources like iron and silicon, build their own rocket and set out to rescue other colonies, balancing limited oxygen, fuel and rocket mass along the way. This mirrors NASA’s real idea of in-situ resource utilization, which the MOXIE experiment demonstrated by making oxygen from Mars air. Every choice has a cost, so players learn to plan, think like engineers and take responsibility for their decisions. Our message is clear: Earth’s story in our game is a warning, not a prediction. If players learn to protect a new world, they may also learn to protect this one.
details:
What it does and how it works
Beyond Earth: The Last Hope is an educational space mission game set in 2150. Humanity ignored warnings about climate change, resource depletion and pollution, and Earth became uninhabitable. The player is a commander whose emergency colony ship went off course and crash-landed on an unknown planet. In our playable demo, the player explores the planet, collects iron and silicon from rocks, builds a rocket at the launch pad when the recipe is complete (3 iron + 2 silicon), then boards it, launches and flies it freely. Our next steps are managing oxygen and fuel, rocket mass that grows with every part and passenger, unexpected events, and rescue missions on other planets.

Benefits and intended impact
Instead of only reading about space missions, students make decisions with limited resources and live with the consequences. The game builds planning under limits, engineering thinking, scientific reasoning, responsible decision-making and teamwork. It is designed for secondary school and first-year university students, played in class through a short briefing, team play and a reflection discussion. We plan to measure learning with a short quiz before and after playing. Our message: if players learn to protect a new world, they may also learn to protect this one.

Tools and technology
We built the game in Unreal Engine 5 with C++ (Visual Studio 2022) on Windows PCs, using Niagara for visual effects. We used NASA 3D Resources models, a planet surface map and free assets from the Epic Games Fab marketplace. We used the AI assistant Claude to help write the C++ code, suggest assets and prepare the presentation. All design decisions were made by our team.

Creativity
Our core mechanic is based on a real NASA concept, in-situ resource utilization (ISRU): using materials found on another world instead of bringing everything from Earth. NASA’s MOXIE experiment demonstrated this by producing oxygen from Mars air. We turned this idea into a survival story, so learning happens through gameplay rather than being added on top.

Factors we considered
We clearly separated fiction from real science, kept the controls simple for students without gaming experience, focused on a small working demo within the hackathon time, used only freely licensed assets with credits, and followed the competition rules on logos, personal information and AI disclosure.
dataRefs: NASA’s Oxygen-Generating Experiment MOXIE Completes Mars Mission
